title: Recruiting screen - Alexandra Patel
summary: Initial 35-minute phone screen for a SWE candidate role on the inference/runtime team. Reviewed background, past projects (distributed inference, caching, quantization), asked behavioral and system-design-lite questions. Candidate to receive take-home exercise; hiring team to review and schedule next step if pass.
topics: Inference runtime and distributed systems experience
action_items: Samantha Lee - Send take-home coding exercise + scheduling links - due 2025-07-11
Mark Rivera - Share initial screen notes and recommend next-step timing with hiring committee - due 2025-07-12
next_steps: Candidate to complete take-home challenge within 4 days
If exercise passes, schedule onsite loop with engineering team (approx 2 weeks)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-10 14:00 UTC | Duration: 35 minutes | Attendees: Mark Rivera, Samantha Lee (Redwood) - Alexandra Patel (Candidate)

[00:00] Samantha: Hi Alexandra, thanks for taking time. I'm Samantha from recruiting at Redwood Inference. This is a 30 minute screen, Mark Rivera will do the technical questions. Quick intro, then Mark will ask a few technical things and we wrap with next steps. Sound good?
[00:10] Alexandra: Yes, that works, thanks for having me.
[00:15] Mark: Hey Alex, nice to meet you. I'm Mark, hiring manager on the inference/runtime team. How are you today?
[00:20] Alexandra: Doing well, excited to chat.
[00:25] Mark: Great. Can you give me a 2-3 minute walk through your resume, highlight the projects most relevant to serving and inference?
[00:35] Alexandra: Sure. I was at FluxAI for three years, worked on their model serving infra, mostly on the runtime that orchestrated GPUs and managed KV cache for transformer models. I led a project to implement prefix caching which reduced average token compute by about 18% on our customer workloads. Before that I was at DataLayer building distributed batch pipelines. I also did some quantization experiments—converted some models to int8 using a custom pipeline and measured latency and quality tradeoffs, mostly on V100s.
[01:10] Mark: Nice, the prefix caching number is interesting. Can you explain how you designed the cache eviction policy and what metrics you used to choose it?
[01:20] Alexandra: Yeah, we used an LRU-ish policy but augmented it with access frequency and sequence-length heuristics. So items that were both recent and frequently reused got sticky weight. We tracked cache hit rate, average tokens saved per request, and also latency percentiles to ensure no tail regression. We rolled out first with a shadow mode to compare metrics before moving to full production.
[01:45] Mark: Did you run into any consistency or memory pressure issues?
[01:50] Alexandra: Memory pressure was the main one; we added a soft limit per shard and used eviction to upstream to cold storage. For long-running chat sessions we serialized old KV segments to S3 and rehydrated on demand. There was a tradeoff with latency on rehydration but it was acceptable for our SLA.
[02:10] Samantha: (quiet)
[02:15] Mark: Okay, can you describe a time you had to trade latency for cost and how you communicated that tradeoff to product?
[02:25] Alexandra: At FluxAI we had a large customer with tight cost constraints; we proposed a tiered routing policy—low-priority requests went to quantized variants with slightly higher latency for tail cases, high-priority went to full-precision. We measured quality delta using a small eval set and presented cost savings numbers; product agreed to a hybrid approach. We also instrumented rollback if quality drifted.
[02:55] Mark: Good. Follow up: how did you measure quality drift practically?
[03:00] Alexandra: We used sample prompts from customer traffic and a holdout set; computed embedding similarity and token-level metric like perplexity approximations and some prompt-specific heuristics. We automated alerts for drops beyond a threshold and would trigger human eval.
[03:20] Mark: Do you have hands-on with GPU runtimes and kernel selection?
[03:25] Alexandra: Yes, fairly hands-on. I wrote scheduling heuristics to choose between fused kernels vs non-fused paths depending on sequence length and batch size. On the infra side I tuned batch windows and saw up to 2x throughput improvements in some workloads.
[03:45] Mark: Sounds relevant. Any experience with private/VPC deployments or on-prem customers?
[03:50] Alexandra: We supported both. For VPCs we had a control plane that could talk to customer-managed infra; we used KMS for key management integration. On-prem required packaging the runtime and some manual steps—networks and firewall setups were the main friction.
[04:10] Samantha: Quick check, Alex are you open to relocation or remote? (brief)
[04:15] Alexandra: Fully remote is preferred, willing to travel for onsite loops.
[04:20] Mark: Cool. Let's do a small system design Q. Imagine you need to build a low-latency inference path for a chat product with many short requests and occasional long contexts. How would you structure the serving?
[04:35] Alexandra: I'd separate hot path vs cold path. Hot path keeps recent chat contexts in memory KV cache with async persistence. Use small batch windows to keep latency low, with dynamic batching when load rises. Long contexts could be chunked and offloaded to cold storage and a fallback to a truncated context for strict latency needs. For model variants, have a lightweight quantized model for default and route high-importance sessions to full precision. Also would employ adaptive kernel selection and possibly use per-tenant routing to avoid noisy neighbor effects.
[05:20] Mark: What about autoscaling? How fast should it be and what signals?
[05:25] Alexandra: Combine request queue length, CPU/GPU utilization, and p50/p95 latency as signals. Use faster scaling for bursts with buffer capacity and cooler downscaling with smoothing to avoid oscillations. For GPUs maybe keep a small warm pool to avoid cold-start costs.
[05:45] Mark: Any familiarity with continuous batching and its pitfalls?
[05:50] Alexandra: Yes, continuous batching reduces overhead for small requests but increases tail latency for single-user sessions. We mitigated this with max-wait knobs per session and per-priority queues. Also instrumented per-request latency to detect regressions.
[06:10] Samantha: (note: candidate has experience with continuous batching)
[06:15] Mark: Tell me about an incident where something went wrong in production and what you did.
[06:20] Alexandra: We had a regression after a kernel change that increased p99 latency for long sequences. Our alerting caught p99 spikes, we rolled back that kernel variant, and ran a bisection on tests to find the offending change. Postmortem: improved our canary strategy and added synthetic long-sequence tests.
[06:45] Mark: Good. How comfortable are you with Python + C++ stack?
[06:50] Alexandra: Mostly Python for orchestration and testing, some C++ for low-level kernels. I've debugged memory leaks in C++ and contributed small kernels.
[07:05] Mark: Do you have open-source contributions or other artifacts you can point to?
[07:10] Alexandra: I have a repo with our quantization experiments and some batching simulators, I can share link after the call.
[07:20] Samantha: Great, please send link in the follow-up.
[07:25] Mark: Behavioral: how do you approach cross-team collaboration when rolling out infra changes?
[07:30] Alexandra: I usually set up a cross-functional plan: docs, migration guides, canary cadence, and a rollback plan. Communicate expected impacts and hold office hours for questions. I prefer working with product to quantify the value and with SRE to test failure modes.
[07:50] Mark: Nice. Quick puzzle: we have a customer that needs sub-200ms median latency for short prompts at 95% of requests on a T4 cluster; what levers would you pull?
[07:58] Alexandra: Use quantized models to reduce kernel time, optimize batching windows to keep small batches for short prompts, ensure kernel fusion for small sequences, pre-warm GPU contexts, and route latency-sensitive sessions to a higher tier. Also consider model distillation to a smaller model.
[08:20] Mark: Any questions for us about team, roadmap?
[08:25] Alexandra: Yes—what does the team prioritize now? How much focus on private deployments vs hosted API?
[08:30] Mark: We roughly split across hosted and dedicated, with an increasing push on Private for enterprise customers. The team is focused on improving tail latency, smarter batching, and better quantization profiles.
[08:45] Alexandra: Sounds aligned with my experience. Also curious about interview loop structure if we move forward.
[08:50] Samantha: Typically an onsite loop with 4 interviews: systems design, kernel/perf deep dive, team fit, and a culture/values conversation. We'll also have a take-home coding exercise prior to loop.
[09:05] Alexandra: Okay. Quick clarifying: the take-home is algorithmic or infra-focused?
[09:10] Samantha: Usually infra-focused with a bit of systems reasoning and a small coding portion.
[09:15] Alexandra: Good.
[09:20] Mark: (brief) Anything else on your side we should know—gaps or constraints?
[09:25] Alexandra: None major. I'm currently on notice period two weeks and can start four weeks after offer.
[09:30] Mark: Great. Wrapping up: we liked the prefix caching work, GPU runtime kernel selection, and incident response examples. We'll send the take-home exercise and ask you to complete within 4 days. Any constraints?
[09:50] Alexandra: No constraints, four days is fine.
[09:55] Samantha: Thanks, Alex. We'll follow up with links and the repo request.
[10:00] Alexandra: Thanks everyone, appreciate the time.

Notes: transcript contains minor stutters and occasional overlap; some product names may be transcribed imprecisely. Candidate to receive exercise and repo link.

End of transcript.
